pamphlet_excerpts: Programming Core Field Standard: You might not think that writing programs could cause injuries (p. 88).

Programming Core Field Standard Principle 2: But in fact, injuries from programming have much in common with sports injuries and can be prevented using some of the same techniques that athletes use (p. 88).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 3: The main programming-related injuries are repetitive stressinjuries, or RSIs (p. 88).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 4: Just as in athletic activities, an RSI occurs whenstress is placed on a joint, pulling on the tendons and musclesaround the joint (p. 88).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Programming Core Field Standard): When the stress happens repeatedly, the bodydoes not have time to recover and becomes irritated (p. 88).
Step 2 (Programming Core Field Standard): The bodyreacts to the irritation by increasing the amount of fluid in thatarea to reduce the stress placed on the tendon or muscle (p. 88).
Step 3 (Programming Core Field Standard): And just as athletes are trained to do, you can avoid issues like the following by developing good habits (p. 88).
Step 4 (Programming Core Field Standard): Proper equipment and preparation are the keys to prevention (p. 88).

pamphlet_excerpts: Historical Origins and Evolution: As of theprinting of this merit badge pamphlet, more than 2,500 programming languages have been developed (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 2: By the 1950s and 1960s, many new languages were being introduced, including BASIC, Fortran, and LISP (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 3: These languagestook programming beyond binary and assembly to allowportability of languages beyond just the processor hardware of the time (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 4: That is, programs written in these languages could runon two or more kinds of processors or with two or more kinds of operating systems (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Many languages, such as Pascal, werecreated to capture new concepts of computer science (p. 18).
Step 2 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Others, such as Fortran and COBOL, were developed to meet specificneeds of science or business (p. 18).
Step 3 (Historical Origins and Evolution): FORTRAN (Formula Translation), originally developed in the 1950s, was among the earliest programming languages (p. 18).
Step 4 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Well-suited for mathematical calculations, FORTRAN was used mainly forscientific and engineering programming (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Programming Core Field Standard: A program is a set of instructions that tells a processor how to do aparticular task (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 2: A programming language is the tool that converts the programmer'sinstructions into a form the processor can understand (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 3: The roots of modern programming stretch back to before the first computers (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 4: Most programming languages have their originsin early efforts to automate machines like calculating machines (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Programming Core Field Standard): Before the development of modern programming languages, developers used binary code, which is the "native language" of amachine/computer (p. 14).
Step 2 (Programming Core Field Standard): These two numerals used in binary language were numeric codes for the operations a particular computer could execute (carry out) directly (p. 14).
Step 3 (Programming Core Field Standard): Binary code allowed programmers to turn pieces of computer hardware (circuits) "on" (represented with a 1) or "off" (represented by the numeral 0) (p. 14).
Step 4 (Programming Core Field Standard): All modern programminglanguages are built off the concept of trying to turn humancommands into binary or machine code (p. 14).
